slides.title: How we'll share projects, and what you vote on
slides.body: One project partner stays at their table, the other walks around to look at other projects. Each person gets to vote on:
items: Most Creative System
Cleverest Device Name
Best use of Adafruit App
Best Overall Solution
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min to brief. Her slide 4, verbatim. Her count parentheticals — (1x12), (2x4), (1x4), (2x2) — are kept here, off the wall: a student reads them as a voting rule (12 votes in one category, 2 in another). If they are meant for the room, say so and they go back on. Page back here at the end of the block to collect the votes. How a vote is cast is not on the wall — hers to say (open question).

slides.title: The demo checklist
slides.body: Today each team will demonstrate their project:
items: Explain what your system does.
Does the system have at least two actuators?
Does the system have at least two sensors?
Does it function correctly with no Bluetooth central connected?
Can it be connected to?
Does the Bluetooth interface function as expected?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 70 min. Lab 9 §4.6's six checkboxes in the lab's words — no deliverable number and no points on the wall. Leave this slide up through the demo block; the walkers' vote categories are one slide back.

slides.title: Wrapping up
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 23 min: 10 the learning objectives (two slides), 8 where to go from here, 5 last things and the close.

slides.title: Review: ENGS 28 learning objectives
items: Break a problem down and construct a modular hardware+software solution.
Use embedded programming techniques to write "bare metal" microcontroller programs in C.
Write interrupt-driven and timer-driven programs.
Read an electronic component data sheet to understand how to use it.
Design and test basic analog electronic circuits.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min. Her slide 6, objectives one to five verbatim; six to eight on the next slide (all eight overflow one glue slide). Her note: "Just to remind you what we did this term. YOU DID ALL THESE THINGS!!! Can you believe it?"

slides.title: Review: ENGS 28 learning objectives, continued
items: Use the key principles and specifications of analog-to-digital converters to accurately acquire low frequency signals.
Use the physical principles and electrical specifications of common sensors and actuators for embedded design.
Communicate data between a microcontroller and sensors/actuators using a few standard protocols (UART, I2C, GPIO).
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min. Her slide 6, objectives six to eight verbatim.

slides.title: Where to go from here?
slides.body: Courses that have been mentioned during ENGS 28:
items: ENGS 21, Introduction to Engineering
ENGS 22, Systems
ENGS 32, 61, 125, Analog and Power Electronics
ENGS 129, Biomedical Instrumentation
ENGS 31, Digital Electronics, and COSC 51, Computer Architecture
ENGS/COSC 50, Software Design, and ENGS 62, Microprocessors
ENGS 26, Control Theory, and ENGS 147, Mechatronics
ENGS 62, Microprocessors in Engineered Systems (next winter)
ENGS 68, Communication Theory, and ENGS 110, Signal Processing
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 8 min. Her slide 7; "next winter" is her phrasing from last year, and ENGS 62 appears twice in her list — both kept as hers. Her note, verbatim: In 21 some projects use Arduinos! 22: set-up for all the electronics courses. If you liked all the electronics stuff (opAmps, etc), then the 32-61-125 track is for you. 129 officially requires 28 as a prerequisite (Kofi teaches it). If you like the digital stuff, 31 is for you. CS 51 is a really nice complement to 31. 31 goes deeper into the hardware, 51 talks about designing a computer's instruction set. How does the machine language work? CS 50: hardcore software design. 62: higher-end microprocessor design course (higher-level processor). 26 control theory (if you like the feedback stuff), 147 mechatronics (microprocessors, feedback etc). 68: if you think wireless is cool, this one teaches you more about the modulation stuff and how it works. 110: broader in scope, also includes digital audio.
